Strong margins against 99 sampled candidates can conceal poor full-catalog ranks. Sampled HR/NDCG can even reverse comparisons between recommenders; increasing sampled accuracy therefore does not establish better catalog-wide retrieval ([Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). A 2025 study evaluates sampling through fidelity to full evaluation, model separability, exposure-bias robustness and agreement with fully observed preferences—useful distinctions when interpreting diagnostic scores ([RecSys 2025](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086)). Research on sequential recommendation also finds random negative sampling favors head items, supporting popularity-stratified diagnosis ([2024 study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)).

Practical diagnostic proposal: freeze each category’s single GRU4Rec model and select reproducible training-prefix/next-item pairs. Encode each prefix once; score eligible catalog items in chunks, excluding padding and previously observed items while retaining the target. Accumulate the number of items outranking the target and maintain a running top-11 list, avoiding a full user-by-catalog score matrix. Report exact target rank, target-to-tenth-item margin, tenth-to-eleventh score gap, and sampled-hit/full-catalog-miss frequency. These are proposed implementation diagnostics, not published findings or replacements for the host evaluator.

Repeat unique-candidate sampling on those same prefixes using fixed diagnostic seeds. Report target-rank quantiles, the fraction of repetitions with a top-10 hit, and hit/miss flip frequency; this measures candidate-sampling uncertainty, not model uncertainty. Stratify by training-only target frequency and history popularity, with stratum counts. Treat high-scoring unobserved items as competitive candidates, not confirmed dislikes. Keep full-catalog and stress-sampled results separate from the unchanged macro validation HR@10; use no additional fitted scorer, checkpoint fusion or test labels.
